evals.name: rd-low-latency-feed
evals.prompt: We need a Rust service that receives market data over UDP multicast (about 2M messages/sec at peak), normalizes each message, and publishes to our strategy engine in the same process. p99 latency from packet to strategy must be under 10 microseconds. We also need to log every message to disk for audit. I was thinking tokio for everything?
evals.expected_output: Pushes back on tokio for the hot path, explaining that async isn't faster per operation and a work-stealing runtime can't bound tail latency. Proposes dedicated threads: a pinned receive/normalize hot thread that busy-polls, SPSC ring buffers (rtrb) between stages, and a cold thread for disk logging that the hot path never waits on, with an explicit policy for when the audit queue is full (since audit can't drop silently, it sizes the buffer for the burst and alarms, or blocks ingest, and says which). No allocation, locks, logging or syscalls in the hot loop beyond the receive itself, cache-padded counters, core isolation as a deployment requirement, and a preallocated latency histogram reporting p99/p99.9. Code follows the no-panic and hand-written error rules.
assertions: Recommends against running the latency-critical path on tokio or another async runtime, with a reason
Uses dedicated threads with a hot/cold split connected by bounded ring buffers
Pins the hot thread and avoids allocation, locks and logging in the hot loop
Makes an explicit backpressure decision for the audit log path instead of an unbounded queue
Measures tail latency (p99 or p99.9) with a histogram rather than averages
Does not use unwrap/expect/panic in non-test code and does not use thiserror or anyhow

evals.name: rd-review-crate
evals.expected_output: A ranked review. Panics first: &body[0..100] panics on short bodies and on a non-char boundary, and both unwraps panic on malformed input. Then: blocking std::thread::sleep and std::fs inside async code; no timeouts on requests; sequential requests (if async is justified at all, run them concurrently with a bound, otherwise blocking threads are simpler); thiserror, anyhow and once_cell are banned (hand-written error enum with context such as the URL, std LazyLock); tokio "full" and #[tokio::main] defaults; edition 2021 instead of 2024; reqwest isn't on the allowlist and needs a # why: (or hyper from the allowlist); no lint table. Mentions running the audit script and gives concrete fixed code.
assertions: Flags the slice &body[0..100] as a panic on short or non-ASCII bodies
Flags both unwrap calls on parsed input
Flags thiserror and anyhow as banned and proposes hand-written error types with context
Flags once_cell as replaceable by std LazyLock
Flags blocking calls (thread::sleep, std::fs) inside async code
Flags tokio "full" and/or the edition 2021 setting
Notes missing timeouts or the missing dependency justification for reqwest
Points out non-idiomatic code, such as the redundant closure in Lazy::new(|| reqwest::Client::new()) or slicing by index instead of using get or iterators
Orders findings by severity with correctness and panics first

evals.name: rd-cli-wordfreq
evals.prompt: Write a Rust CLI `wf` that prints the 20 most frequent words across one or more files (or stdin), case-insensitive. Files can be tens of GB. Output should be `count<TAB>word` lines.
evals.expected_output: A small crate (or workspace if it grows) with lexopt or args_os parsing into typed args, PathBuf/OsString for paths, '-' for stdin. Streams input with a reused buffer instead of reading whole files, handles non-UTF-8 input deliberately, writes through a locked BufWriter and treats a broken pipe as success, sends errors to stderr and returns ExitCode (2 for usage errors). Hand-written error enum carrying the path. Considers parallelism across files with deterministic output order, and mentions the hasher trade-off only with measurement. Includes tests for usage errors and a closed pipe, and a benchmark for the counting path.
assertions: Streams input instead of reading whole files into memory
Writes output through a locked, buffered stdout and handles broken pipe without panicking
Uses lexopt or std::env::args_os rather than clap without justification
Returns ExitCode with distinct codes for usage errors and failures; errors go to stderr
Uses a hand-written error type that includes the file path
No unwrap/expect/indexing panics in non-test code

evals.name: rd-errors-library
evals.expected_output: Says no to thiserror and explains why, then writes a hand-written #[non_exhaustive] error enum (TooShort { len }, Truncated { needed, available }, UnknownKind(u8)) with Display impls describing only this layer and an Error impl. Rewrites the parser without indexing or slicing that can panic (split_first_chunk / get / split_at_checked), with checked arithmetic on 4 + len. Adds tests that match on variants, a proptest that arbitrary bytes never panic and round-trip encode/parse where an encoder exists, and a cargo-fuzz target since the input is untrusted.
assertions: Declines thiserror and explains the reason
Defines a hand-written error enum with Display and std::error::Error impls
Marks the public error enum #[non_exhaustive]
Removes panicking indexing and slicing from the parser
Tests assert on error variants, not message strings
Adds a fuzz target or property test for untrusted input

evals.name: rd-http-service
evals.prompt: Build a Rust HTTP JSON API for a link shortener: create short link, resolve, and stats. Expect ~20k concurrent clients at peak. Postgres for storage.
evals.expected_output: States the concurrency decision (many mostly-waiting connections, so async on tokio is justified). Sets up a workspace (core logic without I/O, a service crate, a thin binary). tokio with only the needed features and an explicit runtime builder, axum and hyper from the allowlist, a database driver with a # why: line. Body size limits, timeouts on every request and DB call, a bounded connection pool, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM and Ctrl-C with a drain deadline, typed config parsed and validated at startup, secrets from the environment, tracing with a span per request, health and readiness endpoints. Hand-written error enum mapped to status codes in one place. Integration tests on port 0 cover limits and shutdown.
assertions: Explains why async/tokio fits this workload instead of using it by default
Enables only the tokio features used (not "full") and builds the runtime explicitly
Sets request body limits and timeouts
Implements graceful shutdown with a deadline
Uses hand-written error types mapped to HTTP status codes, not anyhow or thiserror
Justifies the non-allowlisted database crate with a # why: comment
Uses a Cargo workspace with a core crate free of I/O
